article.title: From A/B Test to Incrementality: What the Control Group Actually Protects You From
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven business decisions.

paragraphs.en: An A/B test is often summarized as a comparison between treatment and control conversion rates. The deeper purpose of the control group is to estimate a counterfactual: what would have happened to comparable treated customers without treatment. Without that counterfactual, an increase after a campaign can be misleading. Sales may rise because of seasonality, payday timing, weather, a competitor, a holiday, or a broad economic change. Natural purchasing matters too. High-propensity customers may buy even without a message, so counting every purchase after contact overstates impact. Regression to the mean can create another false story when customers are selected after unusually low activity and then improve naturally. Random assignment makes treatment status independent of customer characteristics on average. The incremental effect is commonly the treatment outcome rate minus the control outcome rate. If treatment CVR is 1.20 percent and control CVR is 1.00 percent, the absolute uplift is 0.20 percentage points. Contamination weakens the counterfactual when control customers receive the offer elsewhere or treated customers do not receive the intended exposure. Attrition can also damage the comparison if outcome measurement is missing differently across groups. A contemporaneous control group helps absorb common shocks that a historical benchmark may miss. Stratified randomization can improve precision when segments have different baseline rates. Longer follow-up is useful when treatments shift timing rather than total demand. The central idea is that control customers are the empirical reference for the missing potential outcome, making causal interpretation possible under the experimental assumptions. Assignment and exposure should be stored separately. Intention-to-treat analysis preserves the benefit of random assignment, while secondary exposure analyses can explain delivery failures without casually redefining groups after outcomes are known. Sample-ratio mismatch is another useful diagnostic: unexpected treatment-control counts may reveal implementation errors. When treatment probabilities differ by stratum, the analysis should respect those probabilities and use suitable weighting. Confidence intervals should accompany the point estimate because the control group provides an estimate, not a perfectly known counterfactual. The experiment also needs a stable outcome definition and a pre-specified observation window. These disciplines protect the causal story from convenient choices made after results are visible.
